analysis.one_liner: Caps jury awards, lawyer fees, and lawsuits over injuries from pregnancy care, emergency care, and medical products.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to the floor: a procedural vote to cut off debate and open it to consideration failed 49-48 on April 7, 2004, when 60 votes were needed.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the rules for malpractice lawsuits involving obstetrical, gynecological, emergency, and trauma care. It capped compensation for pain and suffering at $250,000, cut lawyers' contingency fees, made it much harder to win punitive damages, and shielded drug and device makers from punitive damages when their products met FDA standards. Supporters said it would lower malpractice insurance costs and keep doctors delivering babies; opponents said it mainly cut the compensation of injured patients.
analysis.who_benefits: Medical malpractice insurers, hospitals, physicians, and drug and device manufacturers. Insurers and providers face smaller payouts and clearer limits on exposure. Manufacturers of FDA-approved medical products gain near-immunity from punitive damages. Plaintiffs' attorneys lose the fee structure that makes taking cases economical.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insurers, providers, and medical product makers

how_it_helps.text: Caps noneconomic damages—payment for pain, suffering, and lost enjoyment of life—at $250,000 while leaving economic losses like medical bills and lost wages unlimited [S2][S3].
Bars punitive damages against makers of drugs and devices that comply with FDA standards, unless the company lied to the FDA or paid off an FDA official [S2][S3].
Caps lawyers' contingency fees on a sliding scale starting at 40% of the first $50,000 and dropping to 15% of any recovery over $600,000 [S2][S3].
Reduces any award by the value of benefits the patient receives from health insurance, workers' compensation, or other programs, ending 'double recovery' of costs already covered [S2][S3].
Requires punitive damages be proven by clear and convincing evidence of malicious intent, and caps them at the greater of twice the economic damages or $250,000 [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Patients and families injured during pregnancy, childbirth, or emergency and trauma care. A $250,000 cap hits hardest those with the smallest economic losses—newborns with lifelong injuries, stay-at-home parents, and retirees—whose harm is mostly pain and suffering. Reducing awards by insurance benefits takes away compensation people effectively already paid for through premiums.

drawbacks.text: A flat $250,000 cap on pain-and-suffering compensation means a newborn injured for life, an elderly patient, or a stay-at-home parent receives the same maximum as anyone else, however severe the harm [S3].
Reducing awards by the value of insurance and other benefits means patients give up compensation they or their families paid premiums to obtain [S3].
Strict expert-witness and fee limits could make it uneconomical for lawyers to take valid, hard-to-prove cases, leaving seriously injured patients without a remedy [S2].
It would override state law that is more protective of patients, preemption supporters of states' rights might object to on principle [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters argued that high malpractice premiums were driving obstetricians and emergency physicians out of practice, and that capping awards would hold premiums down and keep services available. The cost falls on the small share of patients with the most severe, least-quantifiable injuries: for them the bill substitutes a fixed $250,000 for a jury's judgment of their full loss, and takes back insurance benefits. The proposed gains in insurance premiums and access were indirect and did not accrue to the people paying the bill.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate voted 49-48 to cut off debate on even bringing the bill up—short of the 60 votes needed—so it was withdrawn and never reached a vote on the merits.

narrative.text: Republican Senator Judd Gregg of New Hampshire introduced the bill on March 12, 2004, and it was placed on the Senate calendar [S1][S5].
On April 7, 2004, a cloture vote on the motion to proceed—the step needed to cut off debate and start considering the bill—failed 49-48, with 60 votes required [S5][S6].
The vote split almost entirely by party: 48 of 51 Senate Republicans voted to proceed, while 44 of 48 Senate Democrats voted against, with 1 Democrat in favor and 1 independent opposed [S6].
After the failed vote, the motion to proceed was withdrawn and the bill received no further action before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured patients kept full access to state-court malpractice remedies, and the plaintiffs' bar kept its existing fee structure. Malpractice insurers, hospitals, and medical product makers did not get the federal caps they sought.

for.name: 48 of 51 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted to cut off debate so the bill could be considered

for.name: American Medical Association and malpractice insurers
for.role: Physician groups and insurers backing tort limits
for.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned for federal caps on malpractice awards as premiums rose

against.name: 44 of 48 Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted against cutting off debate, blocking the bill from reaching the floor

against.name: Association of Trial Lawyers of America
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against caps on malpractice damages and attorney fees

sides.party_line_note: The 49-48 vote split almost purely by party: 48 of 51 Republicans voted yes, 44 of 48 Democrats and the one independent voted no, with a single Democrat crossing over to yes.

industries.note: Caps on pain-and-suffering awards, punitive damages, and fees directly limit the payouts insurers must make to injured patients. Their savings came directly out of patients' recoveries.

The bill barred punitive damages against makers of FDA-approved products used in obstetric, emergency, and trauma care, giving them a federal shield. An exception applied if a company misled the FDA or bribed an official.
Providers faced smaller malpractice exposure under the bill, and supporters argued lower premiums would keep obstetricians practicing. Patients' compensation was the offsetting cost.

Sliding caps on contingency fees and limits on damages reduce the economics of taking malpractice cases. When this industry loses in this bill, patients lose their main avenue for suing negligent providers.
